newsitem.title: UK: Emerging Eurobonds falter on currency woes.
newsitem.headline: Emerging Eurobonds falter on currency woes.

text.p: Yield spreads of emerging market Eurobonds have widened sharply amid fears of further currency devaluations, this time in Brazil and Poland, after upheavals elsewhere, bankers said on Wednesday.

"In light of recent devaluations in the Czech Republic, Thailand and the Philippines, the further currency turmoil has cast a dark cloud over emerging markets," a dealer at a U.S. bank in London said.
"From around 1600 GMT on Tuesday (Eurobond) spreads began to climb, by around 10 to 20 b.p. across the board," another trader said.
Dealers said new bond issues would be put on ice until sentiment improved. The volatility caused Argentina to delay the launch of a planned $750 million global bond it announced on Monday.

Argentina's 2001 bonds were quoted at a 175/170 b.p. yield spread over U.S. Treasuries at 1130 GMT on Wednesday, up 30 b.p. from late last week. Its 2006 dollar bonds were at a 275/270 b.p. spread, against 250/245 b.p. last week.
In eastern Europe, Russia's 2001 dollar bonds were trading at 272 b.p. over from 260 b.p. on Tuesday. Russian bank SBS-Agro's 2000 bonds were quoted at 424 b.p. over from 415 b.p. on Tuesday.

An analyst at a European bank said: "A big wave of uncertainty has come over the emerging market sector in general, triggered by two events. One is the fear of devaluation in Brazil. The other is concern over the Polish zloty, which suffered its sharpest one-day fall."

Rumours that Brazil, Latin America's largest economy, might allow its currency to fluctuate shook markets in the region on Tuesday, with debt and equities falling. Brazil faces a growing trade gap, lax government spending controls and, some analysts said, a currency overvalued by up to 20 percent.
Brazilian Planning Minister Antonio Kandir ruled out on Tuesday any change to the government's foreign exchange policy.

On Tuesday the zloty lost five percent against a basket of currencies, although it firmed slightly in early trade on Wednesday. An International Monetary Fund official said Poland's economic fundamentals did not justify such a steep fall of the currency.
Thai and Philippine authorities at first denied they were going to devalue, but both allowed their currencies to fall in what traders said were de facto devaluations.

"The market is volatile and there is nervousness on the part of investors... (so) Argentina has decided to hold off and watch the market," a banker familiar with that transaction said. "The market is not competely closed for emerging market borrowers, but investors are very wary of what is going on," he said.
Sentiment towards emerging market borrowers had improved sharply over recent months due to improving economic fundamentals and better credit ratings.
In the first half of 1997 they raised nearly $58 billion on the international bond markets, according to Capital DATA Bondware, compared with $36 billion in the first six months of 1996.
